content.title: See how Artemis launch returns humans to the moon after five-decade absence
content.text: Humanity is headed back to the lunar surface for the first time in more than a half century — but first, a flyby.Four astronauts will orbit the moon during NASA's Artemis II mission, set to launch the Orion spacecraft from the agency's Kennedy Space Center in Florida on Wednesday, April 1. Along the way, the crew will test systems designed to sustain life during deep-space travel and a permanent lunar presence.This mission is the second in a program that will ultimately land astronauts on the moon's surface and construct a base there.Artemis has faced multiple setbacks because of technical problems, including hydrogen leaks that required rolling the massive rocket back for repairs. But these have been brief delays compared with the long wait since the agency's last Apollo mission in 1972.Here's a closer look at how Orion's crew and hundreds of ground support personnel are set to make history:"Too many years have passed for me to still be the last man to have left his footprints on the Moon," wrote Apollo 17 astronaut Gene Cernan in his autobiography. "I believe with all my heart that somewhere out there is a young boy or girl with indomitable will and courage who will lift that dubious distinction from my shoulders and take us back where we belong. Let us give that dream a chance."These four adventurers are bringing humanity one step closer to answering Cernan's call:The astronauts have been training for this mission since June 2023. Unlike spacecraft that travel to the International Space Station, Orion will have no safe harbor or ability to be back on Earth within hours of a problem. Crew members are not only prepared for this scenario, they have worked to understand all systems well enough to adapt to many challenges.The astronauts studied medical operations to prepare for emergencies and photography to capture images of the moon. They trained in a large pool for their recovery in the Pacific Ocean and with a flight simulator.Back to the moon, and beyond to Mars"We leave as we came, and God willing, we shall return, with peace and hope for all mankind," Cernan said as he departed the lunar surface in 1972.More than 50 years later, NASA's stated goals for the Artemis missions include scientific discovery, economic benefit, inspiration for a new generation of explorers, establishment of a global alliance, and deep-space exploration for the benefit of all.Artemis I, launched in 2022, was an unmanned mission that traveled 268,563 miles from Earth and surpassed Apollo 13 for the longest distance traveled by a spacecraft designed to carry humans.Artemis II will launch from NASA's Launch Complex 39B, the same one used for Saturn V, space shuttle and Ares missions.Though the Artemis II rocket is not as tall as Apollo's Saturn V or SpaceX's Starship, NASA says it is equipped with the largest, most powerful solid propellant boosters that have ever flown.Each stands 17 stories tall, burns about 6 tons of propellant each second, and generates more thrust than 14 four-engine jumbo commercial airliners combined.Artemis III, scheduled for 2027, will fly in low-Earth orbit and test one or both commercial landers from SpaceX and Blue Origin.Artemis IV, scheduled for early 2028, is intended to be the program's first moon landing. After reaching lunar orbit, the crew will transfer from Orion to a commercial lander for their descent to the surface.Artemis V, another trip to the lunar surface planned for late 2028, will be followed by yearly missions.Life on OrionAfter reaching orbit, the crew will exercise and spend time rearranging Orion's interior into a functional space for four people to live and work in zero gravity. They can remove their spacesuits and change into regular clothing.The astronauts will stay clean by using the hygiene bay next to the crew area. Orion's restroom, known as the Universal Waste Management System (UWMS), which was not available to Apollo crews, is a compact, titanium, vacuum-based toilet designed for microgravity. It uses suction to pull urine and feces into separate containers. Feces are stored and urine is vented into space. The system features a privacy stall and an ergonomic seat, and airflow starts automatically when opened. This system is similar to the one in use on the International Space Station.Mission will take historic items back to the moonThe Artemis II flight kit includes several artifacts that reflect the nation’s long-standing dedication to aerospace innovation and exploration, including a square inch of muslin fabric from the original Wright Flyer, the world’s first powered, heavier-than-air flying machine.Pieces of the Wright Flyer have a long history of visiting space, from the wood and fabric that Neil Armstrong carried to the moon on Apollo 11 to the pieces that were attached to NASA's Ingenuity helicopter when it took flight on Mars in an area named Wright Brothers Field by the space agency.Display of the wood and fabric pieces of the Wright Flyer that Apollo 11 astronaut Neil Armstrong took to the moon. Image: Courtesy National Air and Space MuseumThe mission will also carry a 13-by-8-inch American flag that rode along on the very first shuttle mission (STS-1), the final shuttle mission (STS-135), and NASA’s first crewed test flight of SpaceX’s Crew Dragon. Another American flag, intended for the Apollo 18 mission canceled in 1970, will finally embark on its long-awaited journey to space aboard Artemis II.NASA is also sending a copy of a photo negative from the 1964 Ranger 7 mission. The Ranger program launched a robotic spacecraft that beamed images of the lunar surface back to Earth before intentionally crashing into the moon, helping identify safe landing sites for the Apollo astronauts.Finally, an SD card with millions of names from the “Send Your Name to Space” campaign will bring the public along on the lunar voyage.Sample boarding pass from NASA's "Send Your Name to Space" campaign.Tickets to view the Artemis II launch in person are sold out, so your best bet is to watch it live online or on television. You can watch the launch on NASA’s YouTube channel and on NASA's X account. The launch schedule can be found here. Ahead of the launch, NASA is maintaining a 24/7 live feed of the Space Launch System rocket from the Kennedy Space Center in Florida.SOURCES USA TODAY Network reporting and research; NASA; Space.com; © Mapcreator.io | © OSM.org
